title: Risk-adapted MRI Protocols for the Detection of Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer.
abstract: Purpose To compare the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of three MRI protocols for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) according to prebiopsy risk. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 390 male patients who underwent prostate multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) between January 2019 and April 2024 for suspected csPCa, followed by biopsy. Patients were stratified by Rotterdam Prostate Cancer Risk Calculator score into low-risk (<4%), intermediate-risk (4%-9%), and high-risk (≥10%) groups. Three datasets were generated from each examination: mpMRI (T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging [DWI], and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging), unenhanced MRI (multiplanar T2-weighted imaging and DWI), and short MRI (axial T2-weighted imaging and DWI). Overall, 1170 datasets were randomly assigned to 10 expert radiologists (117 examinations each). Diagnostic performance for grade group 2 or greater cancer and clinical utility metrics were compared across risk groups. Results Among the 390 patients (median age, 66 years [IQR, 61-71 years]), csPCa prevalence was 34.4% (134 of 390). In low-risk patients, short MRI demonstrated the highest sensitivity (95% [21 of 22]), with no significant differences among protocols (all P ≥ .21) and greatest potential for safe biopsy avoidance (84 biopsies avoided per missed csPCa). In intermediate-risk patients, mpMRI showed higher sensitivity (83% vs 72% for unenhanced MRI and 62% for short MRI; P = .012 for mpMRI vs short MRI) and higher biopsy efficiency (1.11 vs 0.85 for mpMRI vs unenhanced MRI). In high-risk patients, protocol-related differences were minimal (all P ≥ .12). Conclusion mpMRI was associated with improved sensitivity and biopsy efficiency in intermediate-risk patients, whereas protocol differences were limited in low- and high-risk groups; these findings support risk-adapted selection of MRI protocols. Keywords: MR-Dynamic Contrast-enhanced, MR Imaging, Urinary, Prostate, Neoplasms-Primary, Efficacy Studies, Prostatic Neoplasms, MRI, Contrast Medium, Biopsy, Risk Assessment Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Causes of False-Negative Screening Digital Breast Tomosynthesis Examinations: A Multireader Study.
abstract: Purpose To classify the causes and pathologic characteristics of false-negative screening digital breast tomosynthesis examinations. Materials and Methods All false-negative screening examinations at a single center from March 1, 2019, through December 31, 2023, were collected. Seven fellowship-trained breast radiologists independently reviewed the false-negative screening and diagnostic mammograms preceding biopsy. For each mammogram, radiologists recorded the cancer as visible or not visible. Cancers were classified as mammographically occult (not visible on mammogram), missed (visible on screening mammogram), or true interval cancers (visible on diagnostic mammogram only). Between-classification comparisons were performed with the Pearson χ 2 test or analysis of variance. Results A total of 117 female patients (median age, 60 years [IQR, 49-70 years]) with false-negative screening mammograms were included. Most cancers manifested symptomatically (88 of 117, 75.2%) a median of 237 days (IQR, 187-301 days) after screening mammography. Among cancers, 47.9% (56 of 117), 26.5% (31 of 117), and 25.6% (30 of 117) were missed, mammographically occult, and true interval cancers, respectively. True interval cancers were more often estrogen receptor- (50.0% [15 of 30] vs 16.1% [five of 31] vs 21.8% [12 of 55]) and progesterone receptor-negative (66.7% [20 of 30] vs 22.6% [seven of 31] vs 35.7% [20 of 56]) than mammographically occult and missed cancers. Mammographically occult cancers were more often stage T0 (32.3% [10 of 31] vs 7.1% [four of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and detected at MRI (48.4% [15 of 31] vs 3.6% [two of 56] vs 10.0% [three of 30]) and developed in younger female patients (51 vs 62 vs 59 years of age, all P < .05) than missed and true interval cancers. Conclusion Half of false-negative screening mammograms were missed, one-quarter were true interval, and one-quarter were mammographically occult cancer, with differences in pathologic characteristics. Keywords: Mammography, Screening © RSNA, 2026 See also the commentary by Elahi and Slanetz in this issue.

title: Robotic Flexible Ureteroscopy: A Step-by-Step Guide to the ILY® Platform.
abstract: Introduction Robotic flexible ureteroscopy (rfURS) is emerging as an alternative to manual flexible ureteroscopy for the treatment of upper urinary tract stones. Contemporary guidelines and reviews describe its potential ergonomic and radiation-related advantages, as well as comparable surgical outcomes (1-5). Initial clinical and simulation studies with the ILY® platform have demonstrated feasibility, safety, and a short learning curve, although standardized implementation remains limited (6-10). This video presents a step-by-step workflow for the safe and efficient use of the ILY® platform. Materials and methods A 43-year-old woman with a previous right double-J stent placed for obstructive pyelonephritis underwent rfURS for a 13-mm renal pelvic stone (1,497 HU; volume 1,214 mm³). The video demonstrates operating-room setup, robot calibration and sterile draping, robot positioning and fixation, docking to the ureteral access sheath and ureteroscope assembly, console-controlled navigation, laser lithotripsy, systematic renal inspection, and standardized undocking. A flexible suction sheath was used throughout the procedure. Results Draping and docking times were 167 and 645 seconds, respectively. Robotic console time was 115 minutes, including 52 minutes of laser lithotripsy at 8 Hz and 1.2 J. Basket extraction was not required. Undocking was completed in 74 seconds, and total operative time was 130 minutes. No intraoperative complications or troubleshooting events occurred. Postoperative day-1 computed tomography confirmed stone-free status. The patient was discharged at 36 hours postoperatively without complications, as graded by the Clavien-Dindo classification (11). Surgeon satisfaction was rated 8 out of 10. Conclusion rfURS using the ILY® platform was feasible, safe, and effective. A standardized step-by-step workflow may facilitate adoption, improve procedural consistency, and enhance surgeon ergonomics (12). rfURS represents a meaningful step toward autonomous surgery (13).

title: Outcome of Children Treated with Rituximab for Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome: Renal Histopathology as a Response Marker.
abstract: Background Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) in children remains a major therapeutic challenge. Although calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs) are commonly used as first-line therapy, a substantial proportion of patients fail to achieve remission, and prolonged use may result in nephrotoxicity. Rituximab has emerged as a potential therapeutic option for refractory SRNS; however, treatment responses appear variable, and the influence of underlying renal histopathology remains incompletely understood. Objectives To evaluate the association between renal histopathological findings and clinical response to rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS). Methods Study Design and Setting:This prospective observational study was conducted between 2011 and 2020 at a university-affiliated tertiary pediatric nephrology center. The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of rituximab in children with calcineurin inhibitor-resistant steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and to examine the association between renal histopathological findings and treatment response. Twenty-four children aged 2-12 years were enrolled.Follow-up:Patients were followed prospectively after completion of rituximab therapy through regular clinical and laboratory assessments. The mean follow-up duration after the last rituximab infusion was 5.1 years (range: 6 months-8 years).Treatment Response Definitions:Complete remission was defined according to International Pediatric Nephrology Association (IPNA) recommendations as a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) ≤20 mg/mmol (≤0.2 mg/mg) or negative/trace proteinuria on dipstick testing on at least three consecutive occasions.Partial remission was defined as a UPCR >20 mg/mmol but <200 mg/mmol together with serum albumin ≥30 g/L.No response was defined as failure to achieve either complete or partial remission.Genetic Evaluation:Genetic testing was performed in all patients with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), classic minimal change disease (MCD), and MCD with IgM deposition. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with monogenic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome were identified in the tested patients. Genetic testing was not performed in patients with IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, C1q nephropathy, or dense deposit disease. Results Twenty-four children with SRNS were included (13 males and 11 females; age range 2-12 years). Histopathological diagnoses included focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) in 9 patients (37.5%), minimal change disease (MCD) in 4 (16.7%), MCD with IgM deposition in 6 (25.0%), dense deposit disease in 2 (8.3%), membranous nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), IgA nephropathy in 1 (4.2%), and C1q nephropathy in 1 (4.2%). Overall, 10 patients (41.7%) achieved complete remission and 3 (12.5%) achieved partial remission, predominantly among patients with MCD and MCD with IgM deposition. Responses were uncommon among patients with FSGS. Eleven patients (45.8%), all of whom were non-responders, progressed to end-stage kidney disease. No major adverse effects of rituximab were observed; mild infusion reactions occurred in three patients and mild cellulitis in one patient. Conclusion In this cohort of children with refractory SRNS, favorable responses to rituximab were observed predominantly among patients with CNI- resistant MCD and MCD with IgM deposition, whereas responses among patients with FSGS were uncommon. These findings suggest that renal histopathology may help identify patients more likely to benefit from rituximab therapy; however, the small sample size, heterogeneous histopathological distribution, and observational study design preclude definitive conclusions. Larger prospective multicenter studies incorporating comprehensive genetic evaluation are required to determine whether histopathology can serve as a reliable predictor of rituximab responsiveness.

title: Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Learning (PPP-FL) for Medical Imaging
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that reduces transmission costs, mitigates cross-border data sharing restrictions, and enhances privacy by keeping raw data on local devices. Clients in FL systems train local models and share only updates, which are aggregated by a central server. While this setup limits direct data exposure, FL remains vulnerable to privacy attacks. Existing attack and defense strategies have largely been developed for centralized systems, and adapting them to FL introduces new challenges due to its unique architecture and training workflow. In this work, we first propose a model inversion attack on FL systems using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) in the context of large-scale medical imaging. Our method operates under realistic assumptions about the attacker's knowledge and capabilities. We then examine the effect of client-side differential privacy (DP) in mitigating privacy leakage and incorporate personalized FL to improve model performance under DP settings. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that DCGAN-based attacks can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, revealing significant risks to the privacy of training data. Applying DP reduces attack success but introduces an accuracy trade-off, which is further overcome by personalized FL at each client side. We also evaluate how different aggregation algorithms affect both attack vulnerability and defense effectiveness, underscoring the critical role of aggregation strategies. The proposed attack-and-defense framework is model-agnostic and applicable to a wide range of FL-based systems.

title: DART: Scaling a Shape Representation Across Anatomical Classes and Imaging Modalities
abstract: Current state-of-the-art segmentation models still produce anatomically implausible shapes, such as broken vessels and fragmented glands, on the structures that are hardest to segment. Learned shape representations capture what structures look like and can help correct these errors, but most cover a fixed set of anatomical classes. Extending this coverage across classes and imaging modalities is costly because it often requires new voxel-level annotations. We propose Diffusion for Anatomical Reshaping with Text (DART), which learns a shared shape representation from segmentation probabilities. It uses anatomical descriptions to correct these probabilities without receiving medical images. Across 13 public benchmarks, absolute Dice gains reach 31% for individual gallbladder cases in CT and 10% for individual prostate cases in MRI. Using existing segmentation predictions, we scale a single shape representation from 50 to 377 anatomical classes without new voxel-level annotations for correction training. The shared representation also corrects four lesion classes absent from training and transfers from CT to MRI without retraining. Corrected labels also improve segmentation models, raising one model's Dice from 57.1% to 67.5%. The same pipeline supports annotations for 45,000 CT scans. These results suggest that sharing shape information within and across classes can reduce the need for new voxel-level annotations when extending segmentation to more anatomical classes and imaging modalities. The model is available at https://huggingface.co/Koushik45/DART-Seg

title: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow: from diagnosis to rehabilitation.
abstract: Background Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (UNE) is the second most common entrapment neuropathy of the upper limb, involving physical medicine and rehabilitation, neurology, orthopedics, and plastic surgery. It results from static or dynamic ulnar nerve instability, cubital tunnel syndrome, or space-occupying lesions. Accurate diagnosis requires thorough history, clinical examination, and selection of appropriate diagnostic tests. Search strategy PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched (January 2000-August 2026) using combinations of "ulnar neuropathy", "cubital tunnel syndrome", "elbow", "ultrasound", "electrodiagnosis", "conservative treatment", "rehabilitation" and "surgery". English-language original studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were eligible; case reports were included only where no higher-level evidence existed. Approximately 220 records were screened; 58 were retained, following SANRA recommendations for narrative reviews. Discussion High-resolution ultrasound provides dynamic, non-invasive, cost-effective evaluation of the ulnar nerve and real-time assessment of compression or instability, and guides minimally invasive procedures such as perineural injections, although the only randomized placebo-controlled trial did not show superiority of corticosteroid injection over placebo. Conservative treatment is usually first-line, although surgery may be required in advanced or refractory cases; comparative evidence shows no clear superiority among surgical techniques, while endoscopic decompression carries a higher complication rate than open approaches. Conclusions This narrative review summarizes current evidence on diagnostic pathways and therapeutic options for UNE, highlighting the role of ultrasound as both a diagnostic and interventional tool, and outlines gaps in the literature regarding standardized conservative and surgical protocols.

title: Variability and bias in the calculation of iodine uptake with an adaptive background subtraction method in contrast-enhanced mammography.
abstract: Objective. This work evaluates variability and bias in the calculation of iodine uptake from contrast-enhanced dual-energy mammography (CEM) images using an adaptive background subtraction method. Approach. The iodine uptake images were custom-generated using weighted subtraction, followed by subtraction of a smooth background estimated by interpolation from neighboring regions outside the lesion (adaptive background subtraction). Three main sources of variability and bias were assessed: differences in breast tissue linear attenuation coefficients, stability of the mammography system, and intra- and inter-observer variability in lesion segmentation. Tissue-related effects were evaluated theoretically. System stability was assessed using weekly phantom measurements acquired over a 4-year period. For observer variability, four radiologists performed two segmentation rounds of iodine-enhancing regions in 40 CEM studies. Typical uptake values were below 5 mg cm -2 . Whenever possible, variability was expressed as the 95% coverage interval (2σ), where σ represents the standard deviation . Main results. Theoretical evaluation showed that tissue composition differences may introduce biases in iodine uptake exceeding 0.5 mg cm -2 , although typical lesion compositions produce biases below the visual detection threshold. Long-term phantom measurements demonstrated excellent system stability over four years (2σ ≈0.2 mg cm -2 , and limit of detection = 0.24 mg cm -2 ), with a 7% change in calibration following a workstation upgrade. In the clinical dataset, the four radiologists achieved high detection agreement when segmenting the primary lesions and greater variability for secondary lesions; the inter-observer variability in mean uptake was approximately 2σ ≈0.6 mg cm -2 . Significance. These findings indicate that iodine uptake quantification in CEM using an adaptive background subtraction method is technically robust, which is a key element for exploring its potential usefulness as an imaging biomarker.

In the clinical dataset, the four radiologists achieved high detection agreement when segmenting the primary lesions and greater variability for secondary lesions; the inter-observer variability in mean uptake was approximately 2σ ≈0.6 mg cm-2.Significance.These findings indicate that iodine uptake quantification in CEM using an adaptive background subtraction method is technically robust, which is a key element for exploring its potential usefulness as an imaging biomarker.

title: Generative modeling of complex-valued brain MRI data.
abstract: Objective. Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction pipelines discard phase information captured during acquisition, despite its sensitivity to tissue properties that are not represented by magnitude alone. The aim of this study is to develop a generative framework that jointly models magnitude and phase information in complex-valued brain MRI data and enables the conditional generation of MRI samples representing normal and abnormal brain tissue. Approach. The proposed generative framework combines a conditional variational autoencoder, which compresses complex-valued MRI scans into latent representations while preserving phase coherence, with a flow-matching-based generative model. Synthetic sample quality is assessed using a real-versus-synthetic classifier, image-space coverage tests, and downstream classifiers trained on synthetic data for abnormal tissue detection. Main results. The autoencoder preserves phase coherence above 0.997. Real-vs-synthetic classifiers yielded low AUROCs between 0.53 and 0.64 for generated phase images supporting realistic phase modeling. Magnitude was moderately distinguishable, with AUROCs between 0.53 and 0.82, suggesting appreciable overlap between real and synthetic sample distributions while also indicating a distribution shift for several sequences. Image-space coverage was broad. On the held-out test split, no consistent directional difference from the matched real-to-real references was detected in any evaluated setting, while the training split showed slight to moderate undercoverage depending on acquisition sequence and tissue condition. In downstream normal-versus-abnormal classification, classifiers trained entirely on synthetic data achieve an AUROC of 0.880, surpassing the real-data baseline of 0.842 on the fastMRI dataset. This advantage persists on an independent external test set with biopsy-confirmed labels. Significance. The proposed framework demonstrates the feasibility of jointly modeling magnitude and phase information for normal and abnormal complex-valued brain MRI data. Beyond synthetic data generation, the framework enables future investigation of how magnitude and phase jointly encode pathology-specific features once sufficiently large raw MRI datasets with fine-grained, pathology-confirmed labels become available.

title: Silver sodium nitroprusside nano-aggregates for ultrasound-activated immunomodulatory therapy of MRSA pneumonia.
abstract: The clinical management of methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) pneumonia is hindered by biofilm infections and cytokine storms. A key challenge is the lack of real-time monitoring tools for the inflammatory microenvironment during treatment. In this study, we developed a theranostic platform (CS@EAgNP) using TPP-modified chitosan to load silver sodium nitroprusside nano-aggregates (AgNP) and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG). This system combines ultrasound (US) imaging with US-activated therapy. The CS@EAgNP nano-aggregates can act as an excellent US contrast enhancer. In vivo US imaging indicated that AgNP generated significantly enhanced echo signals at the infection site, providing real-time and high-contrast visualization of the inflammatory foci that was unattainable with normal lung tissue. Moreover, these nano-aggregates release NO, silver and EGCG under US. The NO and silver penetrate biofilms to kill MRSA, while EGCG scavenges reactive oxygen species and modulates inflammation. This reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and TNF- α , mitigating the cytokine storm. In vivo results further confirm that this image-guided strategy achieves significant bacterial clearance and promotes lung tissue regeneration without detectable toxicity to major organs. This integrated approach bridges diagnosis and treatment, offering a promising solution for managing MRSA pneumonia.

title: The eye in systemic vasculitis.
abstract: Purpose of review This review summarizes the spectrum of ocular manifestations in systemic vasculitis, emphasizing recent advances in clinical recognition, multimodal imaging, biomarkers, and targeted treatment. Recent findings Ocular involvement may precede systemic manifestations and affect the anterior segment, retina, choroid, optic nerve, or orbit. In giant cell arteritis, vascular ultrasound is a preferred first-line imaging modality, while orbital and retinal imaging may provide complementary information on ischemic injury and treatment response. Ultra-widefield fluorescein angiography improves the detection of peripheral retinal nonperfusion in Takayasu arteritis. In antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, particularly granulomatosis with polyangiitis, ocular or orbital inflammation may be the initial or isolated manifestation, and rituximab-based therapy has been associated with favorable outcomes in orbital inflammatory disease. In Behçet uveitis, ocular-specific diagnostic criteria, imaging biomarkers, and treat-to-target biologic strategies are emerging. However, many of these approaches require validation in larger prospective studies. Summary Prompt recognition and multidisciplinary management are essential to prevent irreversible visual loss. New imaging methods and targeted therapies have broadened diagnostic and therapeutic options. Despite these advances, standardized ocular outcome measures and validation of emerging imaging and molecular biomarkers remain important priorities.

title: Artificial intelligence in personalized internal dosimetry for radiopharmaceutical therapy: a narrative mini-review.
abstract: Personalized internal radiation dosimetry supports individualized radiopharmaceutical therapy but remains difficult to implement because workflows require repeated quantitative imaging, segmentation, registration, kinetic modeling, and absorbed-dose calculation. This mini-review summarizes current evidence on artificial intelligence across the personalized dosimetry workflow and considers clinical readiness. A narrative PubMed search was completed in early 2026 and covered peer-reviewed studies published from 2015 to early 2026. Studies addressing artificial intelligence, machine learning, or deep learning in quantitative image reconstruction, segmentation, registration, time-activity curve estimation, absorbed-dose calculation, or clinical decision support were considered. Studies reporting quantitative performance or validation results were prioritized. Deep learning reduced yttrium-90 single-photon emission computed tomography reconstruction error from 149.5% ± 31.2% to 9.2% ± 1.7%; lesion dose-rate error was 8.6% ± 5.7% in virtual-patient testing. Learning-based registration reduced computation time from about 50 s to under 6 s. Single-time-point approaches can simplify imaging, and recent machine learning work has explored prediction of organ effective half-life. Automated segmentation methods show improving reproducibility, whereas evidence for artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support remains mainly retrospective and single-center. Artificial intelligence applications in reconstruction and segmentation appear closer to clinical readiness, while decision-support applications still require prospective, multicenter validation.

title: Novel therapies for glioblastoma.
abstract: Purpose of review Glioblastoma is the most aggressive and treatment-resistant primary brain tumor in adults. Given its clinical severity and biological complexity, research efforts are focused on understanding and targeting intratumoral heterogeneity, adaptive resistance, drug delivery barriers, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. This review highlights emerging therapeutic approaches for the treatment of glioblastoma including advances in radiation planning, molecularly targeted therapy, immunotherapy, blood-brain barrier modulation, and neuronal signaling. Recent findings Radiation therapy remains a cornerstone of glioblastoma treatment, and advances in image-guided planning are being developed to refine treatment margins and improve tolerability without compromising efficacy. Blood-brain barrier permeability is being improved through device-assisted approaches, including focused ultrasound in combination with systemic therapies. Molecularly targeted and immunotherapeutic approaches continue to be evaluated, increasingly with biomarker-informed strategies to optimize patient selection. In parallel, drug repurposing, neuronal modulation, and metabolic interventions have shown promising preclinical and retrospective signals and are moving towards prospective studies. Interventions to improve quality of life are also underway with early palliative care showing significant impact for patients with glioblastoma. Summary As the field moves towards tailored and precision-guided approaches, combination strategies remain central to addressing the multiple mechanisms by which glioblastoma evades treatment.

title: Hydatid Pulmonary Embolism: A 25-Year Single-Center Case Series with Review of Current Management
abstract: Introduction: Hydatid pulmonary embolism is a rare but serious complication of cystic echinococcosis. It most often results from the rupture of a cardiac hydatid cyst into the right chambers or, more rarely, from the extension of a hepatic cyst into the inferior vena cava with embolic migration to the pulmonary arteries. Diagnosis is difficult due to non-specific clinical presentation. Methods We conducted a retrospective study including patients treated for hydatid pulmonary embolism in the thoracic and cardiovascular surgery department between 2000 and 2024. Clinical, radiological, therapeutic and evolutionary data were analysed. Results Nine patients were identified (5 women, 4 men), with a mean age of 39 years (19–64 years). All were symptomatic. The diagnosis was based on chest computed tomography and/or pulmonary angiography. The involvement was right-sided in six cases, left-sided in one case and bilateral in two cases. Six patients had an associated hepatic cyst and two had cardiac involvement. Eight patients underwent surgery (lobectomy, segmentectomy, pneumonectomy or embolectomy with cystectomy). One patient died before surgery due to compressive pericardial effusion. The average length of postoperative hospitalisation was four days, with no immediate complications. At follow-up (6 months to 7 years), the majority of patients were stable. One late death due to acute heart failure occurred at 12 months and one recurrence was observed at 7 years. Conclusion Hydatid pulmonary embolism is a rare condition with a potentially severe prognosis. Surgical treatment remains central. The role of adjuvant medical treatment with albendazole remains to be clarified.

title: Case Report: Primary hyperparathyroidism with intrathyroidal adenoma in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome: The first case report
abstract: The occurrence of primary hyperparathyroidism (PHP) in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is rare. The few cases reported parathyroid adenoma as the origin of PHP. We herein, report the first case of concomitant diagnosis of PHP with ectopic intrathyroidal adenoma and SLE associated with antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). A 43-years old woman presented with deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) medically treated. The etiological screening retained APS associated with SLE diagnosed. Other than that, biological tests revealed hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia and elevated levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH) leading to the diagnosis of PHP. Cervical ultrasound and SPECT/CT parathyroid scintigraphy found a suspect thyroidal nodule with a pathological parathyroid gland. Thyroid lobectomy and isthmectomy histopathological examination revealed inferior intrathyroidal adenoma. Surgical intervention permitted to correct calcium-phosphate disturbances and to normalize PTH levels. Hypercalcemia in SLE patients should be roughly investigated. Even if PHP is a common cause of hypercalcemia in general population, it remains rare in SLE patients. In such cases, ectopic adenoma is exceptional.

title: From Manual to Machine: Development and Internal Validation of an NLP-Based Prediction Model for Brain Death Using Admission CT Reports, 2011–2024
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Early identification of patients progressing toward brain death may reduce missed organ donation opportunities. We aimed to develop and internally validate an interpretable natural language processing (NLP) model using admission brain computed tomog-raphy (CT) reports. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 163 adults ad-mitted between 2011 and 2024 with acute neurological injury; 96 subsequently fulfilled brain death criteria and 67 did not. Predictors were derived exclusively from admission CT report text using rule-based preprocessing and term frequency–inverse document frequency word 1–3-gram features. Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and support vector machine models were evaluated using repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation with 20 repetitions. Vectorization, cal-ibration, model fitting, and threshold selection were restricted to training folds. A prespecified sensitivity target of at least 95% guided threshold selection. Interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). RESULTS: XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.807 (95% confidence in-terval, 0.793–0.820) and a pooled out-of-fold value of 0.791. At the high-sensitivity operating point, mean sensitivity was 0.947 and specificity was 0.275. SHAP identified clinically plausible descriptors related to cerebral edema, mass effect, ventricular distortion, ischemic injury, and midline abnormalities. CONCLUSIONS: Admission CT reports contain prognostic information that can be extracted using NLP to support earlier identification of patients at risk of progression to brain death and potential organ donation. External multicenter validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Study on the Value of pH-Responsive Probes in Evaluating Acidic Environment Changes During Chronic Liver Disease Progression in Rats
abstract: During the progression of chronic liver disease, changes in the acidic microenvironment of liver tissue are closely correlated with the extent of pathological injury, making precise monitoring of these changes critical for disease assessment. Traditional detection methods (e.g., blood gas analysis, tissue pH electrodes) suffer from limitations such as high invasiveness and low spatiotemporal resolution, hindering dynamic reflection of hepatic acid environment evolution. PH-responsive probes (e.g., fluorescent probes, magnetic resonance probes), leveraging their non-invasive, real-time, and high-specificity advantages, have emerged as a research focus in this field. This review focuses on the application of such probes in rat chronic liver disease models: outlining their design principles and types, analyzing their quantitative detection capabilities for liver acidification levels, summarizing their value in correlating pathological processes such as liver inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, and demonstrating their ability to identify disease progression and evaluate intervention efficacy through early detection of acidic environment changes. Studies indicate that pH-responsive probes provide a tool for elucidating the mechanisms of the acidic microenvironment in chronic liver disease and lay the foundation for developing non-invasive monitoring technologies in clinical translation, holding significant academic and practical value.

Traditional detection methods (e.g., blood gas analysis, tissue pH electrodes) suffer from limitations such as high invasiveness and low spatiotemporal resolution, hindering dynamic reflection of hepatic acid environment evolution. PH-responsive probes (e.g., fluorescent probes, magnetic resonance probes), leveraging their non-invasive, real-time, and high-specificity advantages, have emerged as a research focus in this field. This review focuses on the application of such probes in rat chronic liver disease models: outlining their design principles and types, analyzing their quantitative detection capabilities for liver acidification levels, summarizing their value in correlating pathological processes such as liver inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, and demonstrating their ability to identify disease progression and evaluate intervention efficacy through early detection of acidic environment changes. Studies indicate that pH-responsive probes provide a tool for elucidating the mechanisms of the acidic microenvironment in chronic liver disease and lay the foundation for developing non-invasive monitoring technologies in clinical translation, holding significant academic and practical value.

title: All-Suture Fixation for Acute Turf Toe Injuries.
abstract: Background Turf toe is a hallux metatarsophalangeal joint (MTPJ) injury caused by hyperextension of the great toe with axial loading 1,2 . High-grade injuries may threaten return to sport and require surgery 3,4 . Here, we describe a capsular reconstruction of the great toe MTPJ with all-knotless suture anchors and suture tape augmentation for turf toe injuries, in isolation or in combination with a traumatic bunion, designed to reduce suture burden, minimize soft-tissue irritation, and facilitate recovery. Description The procedure begins with the patient supine. A direct medial approach to the hallux MTPJ is performed. Both the medial base of the proximal phalanx and the medial eminence of the metatarsal head are drilled at isometric points, and augmentation with suture tape is then performed. Isometric drill holes are placed in the medial proximal phalanx base and metatarsal head for suture tape augmentation. A knotless suture anchor is placed approximately 3 mm proximal to the articular margin of the metatarsal head, repairing the medial capsule in a horizontal mattress fashion. An additional knotless anchor is placed at the plantar plate insertion, and the suture is passed through the tibial sesamoid sling and tensioned with the toe in 20° of plantar flexion. Suture tape is secured into the proximal phalanx with an interference screw, then passed through the deep capsule into the metatarsal head, followed by the placement of an additional interference screw into the metatarsal head. The anchor is inserted into the plantar-medial proximal phalanx at the flexor hallucis brevis insertion. The toe is flexed during tensioning, then adjusted per clinical examination and the sesamoid location beneath the metatarsal head. Knotless fixation permits incremental tensioning with intraoperative assessment of motion. Final tensioning is performed with the toe in neutral to correct deformity without overconstraint, preserving range of motion. Alternatives Nonoperative alternatives include rest, ice, compression and elevation; anti-inflammatory drugs; activity modification; and brief immobilization 5,6 . Operative alternatives include primary capsuloligamentous complex repair with nonabsorbable sutures, plantar plate advancement with bone tunnels or suture anchors if primary repair is not feasible, and concomitant procedures such as sesamoidectomy and bunionectomy based on the injury pattern 2,7,8 . Rationale This technique is intended for high-grade turf toe injuries with capsuloligamentous disruption, sesamoid complex insufficiency, and MTPJ instability. Nonoperative treatment may be appropriate in cases of low-grade injury; however, persistent pain, instability, or loss of push-off strength following nonoperative treatment would indicate a higher-grade injury. Compared with isolated repair or plantar plate advancement alone, this technique restores both static and dynamic stabilizers of the hallux MTPJ while addressing associated angular deformity. Suture tape augmentation resists recurrent hyperextension and valgus forces while allowing controlled physiologic motion. Knotless, low-profile suture anchors minimize bulk and hardware prominence in a region with limited soft-tissue coverage and bone stock. This construct offers a robust reconstruction option for athletes requiring predictable restoration of stability and reliable return to sport. Expected outcomes Operative treatment of high-grade turf toe injuries has been shown to result in reliable pain relief, restored stability, and high rates of return to sport 8 . Previous studies have suggested improved function and earlier return to play compared with prolonged nonoperative treatment in appropriate patients 6,7 . Knotless suture anchors reduce implant prominence and eliminate knot-related irritation, while the small insertional diameter of the suture anchors preserves bone stock in the metatarsal head and proximal phalanx. This construct provides immediate stability while allowing controlled motion, facilitating rehabilitation, and reducing postoperative stiffness. Athletes typically return to unrestricted activity within 6 to 9 months, aided by the suture tape augmentation allowing earlier movement through the range of motion. This augmentation reduces the need for long-term spica splinting and bracing and reduces the risk of recurrence. Important tips The small anchor diameter and use of suture tape allow easy access without hardware burden.○ Suture choice depends on surgeon preference regarding construct stiffness and on the tissue quality and risk of irritation. We believe that suture tape lays flatter and, if required, knots are smaller.Avoid suture twisting or kinking, which can prematurely lock anchors, compromising fixation.○ After the anchor is placed, we keep the suture tape secured out of the field as we prepare the capsule with absorbable suture. As we load the second anchor, we maintain tension on the tape to prevent twisting.Overtightening the MTPJ capsule may lead to altered biomechanics. title: Surgical difficulty and factors associated with conversion to thoracotomy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy for non-small cell lung cancer: a single- center retrospective study
abstract: Abstract Background: Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy can produce substantial tumor regression in resectable or potentially resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but treatment-related inflammation, fibrosis, and hilar adhesions may increase technical surgical difficulty. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 101 patients with NSCLC who underwent surgery after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy at a single center. Thirty-four patients completed video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) and 67 underwent conversion to thoracotomy. Results: In the principal Firth penalized multivariable analysis, cT3-4 disease (OR 34.33, 95% CI 7.84–150.22), pulmonary artery relationship grade (OR 2.03 per grade, 95% CI 1.09–3.79), and bronchial relationship grade (OR 3.25 per grade, 95% CI 1.35–7.82) were associated with conversion. The cT3-4 estimate should be interpreted cautiously because of sparse non-conversion observations. Pulmonary artery and bronchial grades were also associated with longer operative time. Conversion was associated with longer operative time, greater blood loss, and longer chest tube duration, whereas no statistically significant differences were observed in R0 resection or pulmonary complication rates. Conclusions: Higher clinical T stage and more complex pulmonary artery and bronchial relationships on CT were associated with conversion and technical surgical difficulty after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Preoperative assessment of local tumor extent and hilar anatomy may assist operative planning; conversion should be interpreted as a potential intraoperative safety strategy rather than automatically as failure of minimally invasive surgery.

title: Development and validation of a three-marker urine DNA methylation assay complementary to mpMRI for pre-biopsy risk stratification of clinically significant prostate cancer
abstract: Abstract Background Current prostate cancer (PCa) diagnostic strategies remain limited in accurately identifying clinically significant disease while avoiding unnecessary biopsy. This study aimed to develop and independently validate a non-invasive urine DNA methylation assay using naturally voided, non-digital rectal examination (non-DRE) urine and assess its complementary value with multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa; Grade Group ≥ 2). Methods The biomarker discovery phase was initiated using microarray-based DNA methylation profiling to screen for tumor-specific alterations, and the candidate regions were subsequently validated by bisulfite-pyrosequencing in the same tissue specimens. Three prioritized markers– CDYL , EMX2 , and LRRC4– were incorporated into a linear target enrichment quantitative methylation-specific PCR assay. Marker-specific thresholds optimized in a training cohort (n = 33) were locked and evaluated in an independent validation cohort of men undergoing biopsy for suspected PCa (n = 97). All participants underwent pre-biopsy mpMRI and standard prostate biopsy. Of the 97 validation patients, 89 were evaluable for combined-modality analysis, while 8 were excluded due to missing mpMRI scans. Results In the training cohort, the assay achieved 100% sensitivity and 31.6% specificity for csPCa. In the independent validation cohort, standalone assay performance yielded 75.9% sensitivity and 44.2% specificity. Among the 89 patients evaluable for both modalities (49 csPCa, 40 no-csPCa), mpMRI alone (PI-RADS ≥ 4) showed a sensitivity of 69.4%. Combining the urine assay and mpMRI using an either-positive strategy significantly increased diagnostic sensitivity to 91.8% ( P < 0.01 vs. mpMRI alone), with a negative predictive value of 78.9%. In an exploratory analysis of the indeterminate PI-RADS 3 subgroup, the urine assay correctly identified all 4 biopsy-confirmed cases of csPCa (100% sensitivity). Conclusions The three-marker non-DRE urine DNA methylation assay demonstrates independent diagnostic performance and complementarity to mpMRI. Integrating this molecular assay with anatomical imaging significantly enhances csPCa detection compared with mpMRI alone. These findings support prospective evaluation of predefined, integrated MRI-urine methylation algorithms to refine pre-biopsy risk stratification and optimize biopsy decision-making.

title: Longitudinal intratumoral and peritumoral MRI radiomics for predicting pathologic complete response to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma: a retrospective two-center study
abstract: Abstract Background Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) is an important marker of treatment sensitivity in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), but reliable preoperative prediction remains challenging. This study investigated whether longitudinal intratumoral and peritumoral MRI radiomics could improve pCR prediction and whether integration with clinicopathologic factors provided additional value. Methods This retrospective two-center study included 310 patients with locally advanced HNSCC who underwent NACI followed by definitive surgery, comprising 151 patients in the training cohort, 66 in the internal validation cohort, and 93 in the independent external test cohort. MRI was performed before treatment and after the second NACI cycle. Radiomic features were extracted from contrast-enhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted images within the primary tumor and 1-, 3-, and 5-mm peritumoral regions. Features were selected using reproducibility assessment, correlation analysis, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Pre-treatment intratumoral, on-treatment intratumoral, longitudinal intratumoral, multiscale longitudinal peritumoral, spatiotemporal radiomics, and clinical-spatiotemporal radiomics models were sequentially developed. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration analysis, decision curve analysis, and incremental discrimination metrics. Results Overall, 124 of 310 patients (40.0%) achieved pCR. The clinical-spatiotemporal radiomics model (M6), integrating histologic grade, combined positive score, longitudinal intratumoral features, and 3-mm longitudinal peritumoral features, showed the highest observed discrimination. The AUCs were 0.928 (95% CI, 0.882–0.974), 0.856 (95% CI, 0.749–0.963), and 0.864 (95% CI, 0.780–0.948) in the training, internal validation, and external test cohorts, respectively. In the external test cohort, sensitivity was 0.857 and specificity was 0.845. M6 also showed favorable calibration and net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities. Conclusions Integrating longitudinal intratumoral and peritumoral MRI radiomics with clinicopathologic factors improved preoperative prediction of pCR after NACI in locally advanced HNSCC. The model showed consistent performance in independent external testing and may support individualized pCR risk stratification, warranting further prospective multicenter validation.

title: ‘One shunt fits all?’: A comparative laboratory study of antibiotic- impregnated shunt catheters with retrospective clinical correlation
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Several antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters are commercially available, but direct comparative data on their biochemical and physical characteristics remain limited. Previous observations from our single-centre neurosurgical unit suggested that nominally similar catheter types may be associated with different rates of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain. We therefore conducted a prospective comparative study to investigate potential biochemical and physical differences between commercially available antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters. Methods: Ares®, Bactiseal® and XABO® catheters were compared for antibiotic content, rifampicin degradation products, elution characteristics and antimicrobial activity. Antibiotic elution was assessed during continuous saline perfusion at 20 mL/h and 37°C over 8 weeks, while antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis was evaluated over 60 days. Catheter dimensions, elastic modulus and surface morphology were assessed using three-dimensional computed tomography, nanoindentation and scanning electron microscopy, respectively. An exploratory retrospective quality-improvement dataset from our single-centre unit was additionally analysed to compare the frequency of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain between catheter types. Results: The three catheter systems showed product-specific differences in antibiotic content, rifampicin degradation profiles, elution characteristics, antimicrobial activity, dimensions, mechanical properties and surface morphology. XABO® most closely matched the declared antibiotic concentrations and retained the greatest proportion of intact rifampicin, while Ares® demonstrated the highest sustained clindamycin elution. All three catheters retained measurable activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis for 60 days, with XABO® showing the largest numerical inhibition zones throughout. In the 395-patient retrospective clinical analysis, otherwise unexplained abdominal pain was recorded in 90/182 patients with Ares® catheters (49.5%) compared with 12/108 patients with Bactiseal® catheters (11.1%). After adjustment for age, sex, primary diagnosis, modified Rankin Scale score and activity level, Ares® remained associated with greater odds of abdominal pain than Bactiseal® (adjusted OR 6.89, 95% CI 2.58–18.43; p<0.001). Conclusion: Commercially available antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters showed product-specific biochemical and physical variation, while catheter type was associated with different rates of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain in a retrospective single-centre analysis. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish causality or clinical superiority. Prospective multicentre studies are required to determine whether catheter-specific properties translate into clinically meaningful differences and should influence individualised shunt selection.

title: Bounded Repair Reachability of Residual Critical Blocks in 3D Binary Masks under SAFE-Gated Single-Voxel Flips
abstract: Abstract Critical configurations in three-dimensional binary images violate digital well-composedness, and voxel repairs can conflict with path constraints and foreground preservation. We formulate bounded repair reachability under single-voxel flips preserving the homotopy type of the foreground complex. We establish relations among admissible path sets and show that, under flip-once, endpoint and pathwise fidelity yield identical successful instances and shortest successful depths. Breadth-first search distinguishes found repairs, bounded absence and resource-limited outcomes. On 680 residual blocks from 222 Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2021 masks, unrestricted searches within radius 2 and depth 6 find repairs for 72 blocks under endpoint fidelity and 15 under pathwise fidelity. An endpoint-faithful witness temporarily removes and restores input foreground; a completed search excludes pathwise-faithful repair of that block within these bounds. These results distinguish the topological validity of moves from the admissibility of repair paths. Conclusions are limited to the stated windows, horizons and moves.

title: Optimising neural contrast and minimising tissue shrinkage in dragon lizard brains: buffered Lugol's iodine versus phosphotungstic acid for contrast-enhanced μCT
abstract: Contrast-enhanced micro-computed tomography (μCT) has become a valuable tool for addressing neuroanatomical questions that previously required destructive histology. As a relatively new technique, it remains subject to ongoing technical refinement, and taxon- and tissue-specific protocol optimisation. We evaluated the performance of two common contrast-enhancing agents, buffered Lugol's iodine and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) in aqueous solution, for μCT visualisation of the nervous system in the Jacky dragon lizard, Amphibolurus muricatus by comparing staining time, contrast specificity and brain tissue shrinkage evaluated at three concentrations (1.25%, 2.5% and 5%). Buffered Lugol's iodine outperformed aqueous PTA by requiring shorter staining times (as short as four days) and providing better white matter-grey matter differentiation, whereas PTA required longer incubation periods of approximately three weeks and produced poorer white-grey matter differentiation. Importantly, buffered Lugol's iodine produced higher brain-to-endocast occupancy estimates than aqueous PTA, suggesting substantially reduced tissue shrinkage. PTA-treated specimens exhibited an estimated 13.3% reduction in occupancy and approximately 20% greater brain tissue shrinkage than buffered Lugol's-treated specimens. Together, these findings demonstrate that buffered Lugol's iodine staining provides the high level of internal tissue contrast required to resolve fine-scale neuroanatomical organisation in three dimensions, preserves the spatial relationships among anatomical structures, and reduces artefacts, all of which result in a closer correspondence between the brain and endocranial cavity. From a practical perspective, the study provides guidance for contrast agent selection in future μCT studies and reveals that buffered Lugol's iodine is better suited to fine-scale neuroanatomical, volumetric and geometric morphometric analyses, whereas PTA is advantageous for applications prioritising general soft-tissue or musculoskeletal visualisation.

title: Tracheal Eccentricity is Associated with Respiratory Morbidity and Mortality in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
abstract: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airway remodeling, which may extend to the central airways and alter tracheal morphology. Whether tracheal shape relates to disease severity, quality of life, functional capacity, or survival is not established. Objective: To determine whether CT-derived tracheal lumen eccentricity is associated with cross-sectional and longitudinal clinical outcomes in COPD. Methods: We analyzed 8,383 participants from the multicenter COPDGene study. At each axial cross-section of the trachea, lumen eccentricity (ϵ) was computed from the major and minor axis lengths, and the participant-level value was taken as the arithmetic mean across all tracheal slices; ϵ = 0 denotes a circular lumen and values approaching 1 denote progressively elongated ellipses. Baseline outcomes were spirometry, 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) total score, and modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) dyspnea score. Longitudinal outcomes were annualized change in FEV 1 and all-cause mortality. Multivariable linear and Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for [age, sex, race, BMI, smoking status, pack-years, scanner model]. Results: Tracheal eccentricity rose monotonically with severity of airflow obstruction (0.60±0.07, 0.61±0.07, 0.62±0.07, 0.64±0.08, and 0.64±0.08 in GOLD stages 0 through 4, respectively). Higher eccentricity was independently associated with lower FEV 1 (β = -0.30 L, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.14; p < 0.001), lower FEV 1 /FVC (β = -0.06, 95% CI -0.09 to -0.04; p < 0.001), shorter 6MWD (β = -15.7 m, 95% CI -25.2 to -6.2; p = 0.001), higher SGRQ score (β = 16.9, 95% CI 11.2 to 22.5; p < 0.001), higher mMRC dyspnea score (β = 0.4, 95% CI 0.1 to 0.6; p = 0.007), and accelerated lung function decline (β = -23.8 mL/year, 95% CI -45.13 to -2.48; p = 0.029). Eccentricity was also associated with all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.81, 95% CI 1.01 to 3.26; p = 0.047). Conclusions: Tracheal lumen eccentricity is associated with worse quality of life, reduced functional capacity, accelerated lung function decline, and mortality in COPD, supporting central airway morphology as a candidate imaging biomarker.

title: APOE ε4 Modifies the Association of Left Atrial Remodeling With Brain Aging
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Whether APOE e4 modifies relationships between subclinical cardiac phenotypes and brain structure is unknown. METHODS: In Framingham Heart Study Offspring participants, we related antecedent echocardiographic remodeling (Examinations 4-6) to repeated brain MRI, and cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes to regional cortical morphometry, testing cardiac x APOE e4 interactions with false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction and permutation testing of the regional screen. RESULTS: APOE e4 modified the association between antecedent left atrial (LA) remodeling and subsequent lateral ventricular expansion (beta=-0.00858, P=1.45 x 10^-4, q=0.0023; N=1,305; 3,787 MRI observations), the only FDR-significant result of 16 longitudinal tests, including with participant-specific MRI-time slopes (q=0.034); it weakened when intracranial volume x MRI time was modeled. Four regional ventricular cardiac x APOE e4 interactions met within-family FDR criteria, but their number was consistent with chance (permutation P=0.70). Maximum LA volume index showed an APOE e4-dependent association with left middle-occipital cortical-thickness variability (whole-brain q=0.017; permutation P=0.041) that persisted after ventricular adjustment. Cardiac phenotypes and trajectories showed no FDR-significant APOE e4-dependent associations with plasma Abeta42/40, p-tau181, GFAP, or NfL, and adjustment for these biomarkers changed the regional interactions by at most 3.2%. Allen Human Brain Atlas data showed cholesterol-biosynthesis enrichment in the right superior frontal cortex, implicated by the LV end-systolic volume interaction, but without convergent pathway evidence. DISCUSSION: APOE e4 modified atrial-brain relationships, with the strongest evidence linking antecedent atrial remodeling to later ventricular expansion. Replication with prespecified models is needed.

title: MRI-Trackable Mesenchymal Stem Cells for Oncolytic Therapy: A Clinically Feasible Dual-Labeling Protocol
abstract: Non-invasive imaging of oncolytic virus-loaded mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) could help evaluate cell trafficking and delivery in cancer therapy. Labeling MSCs with iron oxide particles (IOPs) enables in vivo tracking using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study evaluated a dual-labeling strategy that loads MSCs with MegaPro IOPs and the oncolytic virus Delta-24-RGD (DNX-2401; tasadenoturev) and assessed cellular function and MRI detectability. MSCs were labeled with IOPs alone or in combination with the oncolytic virus. We compared cell viability and intracellular iron content among IOP-labeled, dual-labeled, and naïve MSCs, and evaluated differentiation, invasion, and immunophenotype in naïve and IOP-labeled MSCs. We evaluated phantoms containing varying numbers of IOP-labeled MSCs (9 × 10³–1.5 × 10 5 cells) using R2-, R2*-, and R1-weighted MRI, and generated corresponding relaxation rate maps to assess concentration dependent contrast and detection sensitivity. Iron content was comparable between IOP-labeled and dual-labeled MSCs (9.2 ± 2.6 and 11.6 ± 1.4 pg/cell, respectively), with >91% viability across all groups. IOP-labeled MSCs retained invasion and differentiation potential. At the highest labeled-cell concentration, R2*, R2, and R1 increased approximately 4, 2.5, and 1.5 fold, respectively, relative to the agarose control. The estimated detection limits were approximately 2 × 10³ cells for R2* and 6 × 10³ cells for R2 and R1. These findings demonstrate that dual labeling of MSCs with IOPs and oncolytic virus preserves key cellular characteristics while providing MRI-detectable contrast, supporting further investigation of this approach for image-guided tracking of cell-based cancer therapies.

title: Interictal functional ultrasound imaging in human epilepsy resection and responsive neurostimulation surgery
abstract: Over 30% of patients with epilepsy are refractory to medication and may require surgical or neuromodulation-based intervention. Accurate localization of seizure-onset zones (SOZ) and assessment of treatment-associated brain responses remain major clinical challenges. Current workflows may involve invasive intracranial monitoring, prolonged hospitalization, adjustment of anti-seizure medications, and seizure capture to localize the SOZ, while opportunities for complementary intraoperative functional assessment remain limited. We used intraoperative functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) to characterize interictal (i.e., non-seizure) cortical activity in nine patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and to assess treatment-associated brain responses following SOZ resection and responsive neurostimulation (RNS). fUSI signals were acquired directly from the exposed cortex during standard-of-care surgery. We developed six ultrafast power Doppler-based interictal activity markers (IaMs) to distinguish SOZ from peri-resection zone (PRZ) cortex and to quantify treatment-associated changes. The IaMs revealed distinct interictal hemodynamic dynamics between SOZ and PRZ cortex. Following SOZ resection, all six markers changed significantly within the surrounding PRZ. RNS also induced robust, stimulation paradigm-dependent modulation of cortical hemodynamic dynamics. Notably, RNS and surgical resection produced concordant directional changes across five of the six IaMs, despite representing fundamentally different therapeutic interventions. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of intraoperative fUSI for characterizing and distinguishing interictal dynamics within SOZ and PRZ cortex and assessing treatment-associated cortical responses during human epilepsy surgery. Furthermore, fUSI could provide a complementary high-resolution functional imaging approach alongside established clinical methods for SOZ localization and intraoperative functional assessment.

title: Claims-based reconstruction of the pancreatic cancer care pathway links centralization of care to survival
abstract: Background: The organization of pancreatic cancer care may be associated with survival. Using health administrative claims data, we reconstructed the pathway from diagnosis to first-line therapy and examined associations of multidisciplinary team review and treatment at specialized centers with overall survival. Methods: Longitudinal historical cohort study using anonymized health administrative claims data from six Czech health insurance funds, covering approximately 17% of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer nationally between 2018 and 2020. Adults with an incident ICD-10 C25 record confirmed by imaging and histopathology were followed from the index date (the date of the first qualifying imaging or histopathological examination) until death, censoring, or 31 December 2021. Overall survival was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox regression adjusted for age and first-line therapy type. Results: Of 1,255 patients, 920 (73.3%) received first-line therapy and 266 (21.2%) died untreated. Among treated patients, 436 (47.4%) underwent multidisciplinary team review, 335 (36.4%) underwent surgery, and 667 (72.5%) were treated at a complex oncological center. Surgery was associated with longer overall survival than chemotherapy (age-adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.32, P < 0.001). Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer overall survival (adjusted HR 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64-0.92, P = 0.004; crude median 532 versus 394 days). Multidisciplinary team review was not significantly associated with overall survival (adjusted HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.73-1.01, P = 0.073). Conclusions: Treatment at a complex oncological center was associated with longer survival, while fewer than half of patients had a recorded multidisciplinary team review. How care is organized, not only which therapy is delivered, is associated with outcome. The observational design and absence of key clinical covariates limit causal interpretation.

title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
abstract: Background: Ultra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimaging, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. Methods: We systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort(N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. Results: MIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader distinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. Conclusions: Structural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

title: Individual-level Structural Neuroimaging Biomarkers across the Psychosis Spectrum
abstract: Background: and Hypothesis: Although psychotic disorders are characterized by widespread cortical thinning, translating these findings into individualized biomarkers remains challenging. Regional Vulnerability Index (RVI) and Neuroscore are candidate individual-level biomarkers that quantify the similarity between an individual's structural brain pattern and generic psychosis-associated alterations. This study investigated cortical thickness (CT)-based RVI and Neuroscore, along with mean CT deviation from healthy individuals, across the psychosis spectrum. Study Design: Using structural 3T MRI data from 289 participants (clinical high risk for psychosis [CHR], n=39; first episode psychosis [FEP], n=44, chronic psychosis [CP], n=86; healthy controls [HC], n=120), RVI, Neuroscore, and mean CT deviation (z) scores were computed from region-wise CT measures quantified using FreeSurfer v7.2. Group differences and associations with symptoms were evaluated. Study Results: RVI and Neuroscore were significantly higher, and mean CT z-scores lower, in FEP and CP compared with CHR and HC, with moderate-to-large effect sizes (|Cohen's d| = 0.55-1.15). No differences were observed between FEP and CP or CHR and HC. Indices were not associated with psychosis-spectrum symptom severity in the CHR, FEP, or CP groups. RVI (r = -0.561, p < .001) and Neuroscore (r = -0.997, p < .001) were strongly negatively correlated with the mean CT z-score. Conclusions: CT-based RVI and Neuroscore appear to index established disease status but not risk status, while showing substantial overlap with mean CT deviation. These findings highlight the need to further refine these biomarkers through data-driven and multimodal approaches to improve their utility for risk and prognostic prediction.

title: Prevalence and Clinical Correlates of Coronary Perivascular Inflammation in an Asymptomatic Adult Primary Prevention Population: An Assessment of the CT-Derived Fat Attenuation Index Score (FAI-Score)
abstract: Background: Coronary perivascular fat attenuation index score (FAI-Score) on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) quantifies vascular inflammation and predicts cardiac mortality in symptomatic cohorts. However, its prevalence, anatomical distribution, and clinical correlates in asymptomatic primary prevention populations remain uncharacterized. Methods: In an IRB-approved prospective study across two clinical sites, 84 consecutive asymptomatic adults (mean age 53.7 ± 8.6 years; 63.1% men) with no prior coronary artery disease underwent screening CCTA and comprehensive clinical, metabolic, and biomarker profiling. AI-standardized FAI-Score was quantified across three epicardial vessels (LAD, LCx, RCA). High and very high perivascular inflammation were pre-specified as any vessel ≥75th and ≥90th percentiles, respectively. Luminal stenosis and plaque were graded using CAD-RADS 2.0. Results: Elevated FAI-Score (≥75th percentile) was present in 42.9% of participants (36/84; 95% CI 32.8% - 53.5%), with 17.9% (15/84; 95% CI 11.1% - 27.4%) exhibiting very high inflammation (≥90th percentile). Multi-vessel inflammation was identified in 17.9% (15/84), with the RCA most frequently involved (≥90th percentile in 13.1%). Standard circulating biomarkers, including ApoB, non-HDL-C, HbA1c, and PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk showed no association with binary inflammation. Systemic hs-CRP (median 0.8 mg/L) exhibited an inverse correlation with maximum vessel FAI-Score (Spearman ρ=−0.27, p=0.014). Men demonstrated higher rates of elevated FAI-Score than women (52.8% vs. 25.8%, p=0.016; ≥90th percentile: 26.4% vs. 3.2%, p=0.007). Strikingly, 46.2% (30/65) of participants with normal luminal anatomy (CAD-RADS 0) and 47.2% (25/53) with zero plaque burden harbored elevated FAI-Score; all 15 individuals with very high FAI-Score had CAD-RADS 0 (Fisher's exact p=0.018). Body mass index was the sole secondary correlate surviving false discovery rate correction (AUC = 0.71, p=0.001, all-test FDR q=0.028). Regularized multivariable models showed modest out-of-sample discrimination for FAI-Score elevation (cross-validated AUC = 0.71). Conclusions: Coronary perivascular inflammation is common among asymptomatic adults and frequently uncouples from structural plaque and luminal stenosis. Routine circulating biomarkers and clinical risk calculators fail to identify inflamed vessels, highlighting FAI-Score as an independent dimension of primary cardiovascular risk assessment.

title: Leapfrogging cancer diagnostics with AI: a mixed-methods assessment of implementation determinants in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Introduction: Cancer incidence is rising rapidly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diagnostic pathology capacity is constrained. AI applied to routine histopathology could strengthen diagnostic capacity and offer leapfrogging potential by embedding AI into diagnostic systems as they are built up. However, without empirically identifying implementation determinants in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings, AI solutions risk being poorly aligned with local constraints, limiting impact or exacerbating existing disparities. Methods We conducted an exploratory mixed-methods pilot study across three phases: 1) a structured survey characterising the diagnostic and technical landscape and AI priorities; 2) focus group discussions (FGDs) to inductively identify implementation determinants and 3) a second survey quantifying FGD-derived themes. Twelve physicians were purposively recruited (10 from LMIC, 2 from high-income countries for reference) and findings integrated through narrative triangulation. Results There was substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic and AI infrastructure that did not track consistently with country income classification. H&E staining was universally available, immunohistochemistry capacity was rudimentary at 7 of 10 sites and molecular testing absent or minimal at 6 of 10 sites. Whole-slide-imaging scanners were available at 8 of 10 sites, while graphical processing units, required for efficient AI inference, were available at only 4 of 10 sites. The participants would prioritise use of AI for cancer screening, cancer diagnosis, and biomarker prediction from H&E slides. Six implementation determinants were identified: AI literacy, governance frameworks, funding, evidence generation, clinical deployment, and collaboration. Financial constraints emerged as the dominant barrier across all determinants, and collaboration as an important enabling mechanism. Conclusion AI implementation readiness in LMIC cancer-diagnostic settings is highly heterogeneous and cannot be inferred from income classification, underscoring the need for institution-level assessment. Realising the leapfrogging potential of AI in this context requires coordinated progress across all determinants, with sustainable financing, and collaboration enabling the remaining determinants.

title: Optogenetic and sonogenetic pacing of unmodified cardiac tissue upon quick integration with specialized biological actuators
abstract: Electrical stimulation for cardiac pacing has been in clinical use for 100 years and it is the current standard. Alternative scalable pacing methods that are contactless, with good spatial precision and can also be cell-selective are of interest for both in vitro and in vivo applications. Cardiac pacing by light or by ultrasound (US) can be achieved using optogenetic transduction of the tissue and by enhancing responsiveness to ultrasound. In this work we create specialized biological actuators (cell spheroids) out of generic human cells, modified optogenetically (using Channelrhodopsin2) and sonogenetically (using human Piezo1), guide them to a desired location to promote quick integration with unmodified cardiac syncytia within less than two hours. We quantify their ability to confer pacing by light or US and to entrain the native cardiac tissue, modeled here with human induced pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) grown in monolayers, quasi-3D oriented microtissues or cell spheroids. Magnetic guidance (via magnetic nanoparticles) speeds up integration and facilitates positioning to optimize electrotonic load for pacing; size match and three-dimensional growth also accelerate integration. Computational modeling corroborates the possibility to pace by light and by US. Using optogenetically-gated US pulses (0.5 MHz), we show entrainment in voltage and calcium responses and identify the best performing configurations. Experiments reveal the potential role of Piezo1, esp. when activated with Yoda1. The approach is shown to work with physiologically relevant heart cells, such as human cardiac fibroblasts as optimized actuators, and therefore can be considered for in vivo applications as part of heart regeneration efforts. High-throughput cardiotoxicity testing and drug screening in vitro can directly benefit from deployment of such biological actuators.

title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.
abstract: Background The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs). Objective To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations. Design Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective. Setting Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026. Participants No human participants were involved. Measurements Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action). Results The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%). Limitations Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use. Conclusion The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations. Primary funding source None.
